The generic name Aquilops refers to its beak-like snout, derived from Latin for 'eagle' and Greek for 'face'.

The only known specimen of Aquilops, a subadult skull, was discovered in 1997 in the Cloverly Formation of Carbon County, southern Montana.

As an early ceratopsian, Aquilops is thought to have been bipedal.
Basal neoceratopsians like Aquilops likely spent time walking on hind legs due to their small heads and slender arms, unlike more derived forms with larger heads that walked on all fours.
Aquilops was a plant-eater that used its hooked beak to nip at vegetation.

The genus Aquilops was named by Farke and colleagues in 2014.
Aquilops is classified within the group Neoceratopsia.
One study identified Aquilops as the sister taxon of Sasayamagnomus from Japan, suggesting it is one of the most basal neoceratopsians.
Aquilops is basal to a clade containing the Chinese species Auroraceratops and the Mongolian species Yamaceratops, while Liaoceratops from China is more basal than Aquilops.
Aquilops lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 109 to 98 million years ago.
The Cloverly Formation, where Aquilops was found, is dated to either the Albian or Cenomanian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
The Himes Member of the Cloverly Formation, the specific layer containing Aquilops, represents a braided river system.
A 2019 study by Michael D'Emic and colleagues revised the age of the formation to between 109 and 98 million years ago.
